items.question: A family walk keeps splitting up because one person walks much faster. What keeps it one walk?
options: Everyone walks at the slowest pace
The group splits into two walks
The faster walker waits at the end
items.explanation: Looping back means nobody has to be the one being held back and nobody has to be the one slowing everyone down. The fast walker gets extra distance out of the same walk, and the group is never actually apart for long.

items.question: Your cousin finishes her first week of moving every day. Which message is she most likely to keep?
options: I knew you could do it
items.explanation: Three of these could have been sent to anybody, in any week. Naming the actual day says somebody was watching closely enough to notice it. And calling someone a natural quietly suggests the hard days did not count for much.

items.question: A household takes a photo after each session. What is that mostly good for later?
items.explanation: Big days remember themselves. The value of a picture of a completely ordinary Tuesday is that a year later it is the only proof that Tuesday happened at all, and ordinary days are most of what a long habit is made of.

items.question: A nine-year-old wants to race an adult in the family. What keeps that worth doing for both of them?
items.explanation: A head start keeps the finish close, and a close finish is the part that makes a race fun. Letting somebody win says you were not really trying, and children work that out much faster than adults expect them to.

items.question: Two people walking and talking usually end up stepping at the same time. Why does that happen?
options: Footsteps echo and set a beat
The taller one sets the rhythm
items.explanation: Nobody decides to do it. Both walkers make small corrections toward each other until the corrections cancel out, which is the same reason two pendulum clocks on one shelf drift into swinging together.

items.question: A friend two states away wants to keep a daily habit alongside you. What actually makes that work?
options: Doing it at the same hour
Living in the same time zone
items.explanation: What crosses the distance is the message, not the clock. Two people on opposite schedules doing completely different activities can still hold each other to it, as long as each one knows whether the other went.

items.question: A child is copying a movement for the first time. Why is it worth showing it slower than usual?
options: It uses more muscle that way
It makes the set last longer
items.explanation: Whatever tempo you show is the tempo that gets learned, rushed edges included. Going slowly also gives them time to look at more than one thing, so they can watch the feet on one repeat and the hands on the next.

items.question: A house with a toddler in it never gets a quiet half hour. What does moving together look like there?
options: Several short bursts in a day
Waking earlier to fit it in
Taking turns to go out alone
items.explanation: Movement adds up across a day whether or not it arrived in one block. A household with small children is the clearest case where the all-at-once version was never going to happen, and the scattered version still counts.

items.question: You are partway up a long hill and the person with you is struggling. What helps them most?
options: Walking ahead to set a pace
Pointing out the top is close
items.explanation: Matching somebody's pace is support they can feel without a word being said. Walking ahead to pace them turns the hill into a gap they now have to close, and the top is usually not as close as the encouraging version claims.

items.question: What do tag, catch, and dancing have in common that a family workout usually doesn't?
items.explanation: Catch needs a ball, dancing is usually indoors, and only one of the three keeps score. What all three share is that the activity holds your attention while the effort happens behind your back, so nobody has to be talked into minute nine.

items.question: Where along a child's long bones does the lengthening actually happen?
options: In the marrow at the center
Near the ends, at growth plates
items.explanation: Growth plates are cartilage rather than bone, so they show up as gaps on an X-ray of a child's wrist, and a doctor can estimate how much growing is left from what those gaps look like. They harden shut when growing finishes.

items.question: A baby has more separate bones than an adult does. What happens to the extra ones?
options: They harden and are then counted
Each one splits as you grow
items.explanation: A newborn has around 300 separate pieces and an adult about 206. The skull is the clearest case: it arrives as plates with gaps between them, which lets the head through at birth and lets the brain keep growing afterward.

items.question: Why do teenagers tend to fall asleep later at night than younger children do?
items.explanation: The shift starts around puberty and is biological: the sleepy signal simply arrives later in the evening. Teenagers still need roughly as much sleep as they did at eleven. Screens can push bedtime later still, but they are not what started it.

items.question: At what point in life does a person usually have the most bone tissue they will ever have?
items.explanation: After that the body keeps replacing bone but stops adding to the total, so the amount built by then sets the starting point for every decade after it. That is why loading bones with activity matters at both ends of a life, not just the later end.

items.question: What tends to happen to the feeling of thirst as somebody gets older?
items.explanation: The need for water does not shrink; the signal does. That is the reason older adults are often encouraged to drink on some kind of routine rather than waiting until they feel like it, which is the opposite of the usual advice.

items.question: Why does a young child heat up faster than an adult during the same game on a hot day?
options: They have no sweat glands yet
They drink less than adults do
More skin area for their size
items.explanation: A smaller body has more surface compared with the amount inside it, so it picks up heat from hot air more quickly, and children sweat less efficiently than adults on top of that. The shade and the water break matter more for the child than for the adult standing next to them.

items.question: A child's resting heart rate is faster than an adult's. What is the main reason?
items.explanation: A smaller heart moves less blood with each squeeze, so it has to squeeze more often to move the same amount around. A newborn's resting rate can be close to double an adult's, and it settles downward all through childhood.

items.question: Why is getting down to the floor and back up worth practicing as people get older?
options: It is a skill that fades unused
It warms the hips up quickly
items.explanation: Most of the strength and coordination for it is still there. What goes missing is the practice, because adults can spend decades never sitting on a floor at all. People who keep getting down and up keep the pattern available.

items.question: Somebody sleeps the same number of hours as they always did but wakes less refreshed. What changed?
options: Deep sleep takes up less of it
The brain skips the dream stage
items.explanation: The hours can stay the same while the deepest stretch, the part that does the most repair work, gets shorter. Waking briefly more often through the night pulls in the same direction, even when none of those wakings are remembered.

items.question: A toddler learning to walk keeps their feet wide and their arms up. What is that doing for them?
options: It makes them harder to tip
items.explanation: Wide feet and raised arms are the same trick a tightrope walker uses: a broader base underneath and weight held out to the sides. Both habits fade on their own once balance becomes reliable enough not to need them.

items.question: What is the easiest everyday reading of whether you have had enough to drink?
items.explanation: Pale straw usually means you are fine, and darker usually means go get a drink. Counting cups ignores all the water that arrived in food, and lips dry out from wind and cold whether or not the rest of you is short of water.

items.question: Digestion starts in your mouth, before you swallow anything. What is it starting on?
options: It kills germs on the food
It warms the food up first
It adds acid to the food
items.explanation: Saliva carries an enzyme that goes to work on starch straight away, which is why a plain cracker starts to taste faintly sweet if you hold it in your mouth instead of chewing it. The acid arrives later, in the stomach.

items.question: Which part of an apple holds most of its fiber?
items.explanation: Peeling an apple throws away a large share of its fiber along with the peel. Juice is the same fruit with nearly all the fiber removed, which is why a whole apple keeps you company longer than a glass of apple juice does.

items.question: Some vitamins reach you better when the meal has a little oil in it. Why?
options: They dissolve in oil, not water
They are stored in oil only
items.explanation: Vitamins A, D, E and K travel in oil, so carrots cooked with a little olive oil hand over more of their vitamin A than dry raw ones. Vitamin C is the opposite: it dissolves in water and some of it leaves in the cooking water.

items.question: Why are many people thirsty first thing in the morning, having not moved all night?
options: You sweat more asleep than awake
You lose water breathing at night
items.explanation: Every breath out carries water with it, which you can actually see on a cold morning, and a whole night of breathing adds up. Nothing has gone wrong. You simply have not had a drink in eight hours.

items.question: Where does the body keep the fast-release energy it uses at the start of a movement?
items.explanation: Glycogen is a long chain of glucose that the body can take apart quickly. The liver's share is handed out to the whole body to keep blood sugar steady; the share inside a muscle stays in that muscle and is spent there.

items.question: Calcium and vitamin D are usually mentioned together for bones. What is vitamin D doing there?
items.explanation: Calcium that is eaten but never absorbed passes straight through, so the two work as a pair rather than as two separate items on a list. Skin makes vitamin D from sunlight, and some foods carry it as well.

items.question: What is the point of eating something before a long walk first thing in the morning?
options: It keeps you from feeling cold
items.explanation: The liver spends the night handing out its stored sugar to keep blood supplied, so it starts the morning with less than it went to bed with. Food does not become usable energy the moment it is swallowed either, so earlier is easier.

items.question: Your mouth goes dry standing at the start of something you are nervous about. What is happening?
items.explanation: The body's alert setting pauses jobs that can safely wait, and making saliva is one of them. A dry mouth on a start line is a nervous system doing its job, not a sign that you are short of water.

items.question: Bread, rice, and potatoes are all mostly starch. What does that starch become once it is digested?
items.explanation: Starch is a long chain of glucose, so all three arrive as the same fuel in the end; what differs between them is everything that comes along with the starch. Fiber is the chain the body cannot take apart, and that one really does pass through.
